Ornament
OR-nuh-ment
noun
From the Latin ornamentum, from ornare, “to adorn or furnish” — that which is added to a thing to set it off; in Scripture the word is turned inward, and the great ornament is one that cannot be put on.

Biblical Definition

An ornament is a thing added for beauty — the chain, the earring, the bracelet, the crown. Scripture treats ornaments with a striking evenhandedness. It does not forbid them: the LORD Himself decks Jerusalem with them in Ezekiel’s parable (Eze 16:11), Rebekah receives bracelets at the well, and Solomon likens a wise reprover on an obedient ear to “an earring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold” (Pro 25:12). Nor does it flatter them. When Israel sinned at Sinai the LORD commanded, “put off thy ornaments from thee, that I may know what to do unto thee” (Exo 33:5), and the mourning people wore none. Jeremiah’s complaint is that a maid can remember her ornaments better than Israel can remember her God. But the decisive word is Peter’s, and it does not abolish adorning — it relocates it. “Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; but let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price” (1Pe 3:3-4). The contrast is not gold against plainness but corruptible against incorruptible, seen against hidden, priced by men against priced by God. Wisdom too is an ornament of grace unto the head (Pro 1:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

That which is added to embellish; in Scripture chiefly the jewels and attire of a woman, set against the incorruptible ornament of a meek and quiet spirit.

expand to see more

ORNAMENT, n. [L. ornamentum, from orno, to adorn, to furnish.] That which embellishes; something which, added to another thing, renders it more beautiful to the eye.

Hence, whatever confers honour or credit — an ornament to his profession, an ornament to the church.

In Scripture, the jewels, chains, bracelets, and attire worn upon the person (Eze 16:11; Isa 3:18-21).

Israel was commanded to put off her ornaments in the day of mourning after the golden calf (Exo 33:5-6).

The apostle sets the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit above all outward adorning (1Pe 3:3-4).

Key Scripture

1Pe 3:3 — "Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;"

1Pe 3:4 — "But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price."

Pro 1:9 — "For they shall be an ornament of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck."

Exo 33:5 — "For the LORD had said unto Moses, Say unto the children of Israel, Ye are a stiffnecked people: I will come up into the midst of thee in a moment, and consume thee: therefore now put off thy ornaments from thee, that I may know what to do unto thee."

Modern Corruption

1Pe 3:3-4 is corrupted from two sides: an outward legalism that reads it as a dress code and misses the heart, and a modern reading that treats the meek and quiet spirit as an outdated demand imposed on women.

expand to see more

The first corruption is old and churchly. Whole communions have read 1Pe 3:3 as a rule about gold and hairstyles, measured obedience by jewellery, and produced congregations of plain-dressed women with proud hearts — which is exactly the outcome the text was written to prevent. The grammar refuses the reading: Peter’s let it not be is comparative, for the same construction would forbid the putting on of apparel altogether if pressed. His point is where the adorning lives, not what it costs. The second corruption is newer and runs the other way. A meek and quiet spirit is now widely presented as an antique expectation laid upon women to keep them silent and pliant, and the verse is either explained away or resented. But meekness in Scripture is nothing of the kind. It is the strength of the Lord Jesus, who was meek and lowly in heart and drove the traders from the temple; it is Moses’s character, the man who faced Pharaoh. Meekness is power under God’s government, and the promise attached to it is not obscurity but the earth.

Recover the pricing. Peter’s clause is in the sight of God of great price, and that clause is the whole argument. Every ornament is a bid for a verdict from somebody: the woman decking herself for the room, the man dressing for the office, all of it a case laid before an audience whose approval fades by evening. Peter does not say the bid is beneath a Christian; he says it is aimed too low. There is a valuation that never moves, made by One who sees the hidden man of the heart, and He has published His price list — the meek and quiet spirit is great in His sight. So the ornament question is a question of court. Dress for the room and you will be re-priced every season by people who will forget you. Dress the hidden man and you are already wearing what God calls costly, and it is incorruptible, and it goes into the grave and comes out again.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

That which is added for beauty — permitted, stripped in mourning, and finally relocated by Peter to the hidden man of the heart.

expand to see more

Ornament — Latin ornamentum, from ornare, to adorn or furnish.

Hebrew 'adi, ornament or trappings (Exo 33:5; Eze 16:11); livyah, a wreath, in Pro 1:9.

Greek kosmos in 1Pe 3:3 — the same word rendered world, meaning ordered arrangement.

Exo 33:5-6 — the ornaments stripped off from Horeb onward as a token of national mourning.

1Pe 3:4 sets the incorruptible ornament against the corruptible, and God’s pricing against the room’s.

Usage

"Peter relocates adorning rather than abolishing it: the question is where the beauty lives, not what it cost."

"Meekness is not timidity but strength under God’s government — Moses before Pharaoh, Christ in the temple."

"Every ornament seeks a verdict from some court; the only court that never revises its pricing is God’s."
